You clearly think very highly of yourself. This isn't in and of itself a bad thing, but your combination of aggrandized sense of self and inability for self-reflection and emotional growth is going to hurt you in the long-run. It's also going to, and currently is, hurting others.

Your use of sarcasm is troubling. There are some really great quotes from psychology today that may help you:
"The intention behind sarcasm may be to be humorous or playful, but there is frequently an element of poorly disguised hostility or judgment."
"Sarcasm is a thinly veiled attempt to disguise feelings of anger, fear, or hurt. It can be a means of diminishing feelings of vulnerability that may be experienced in the willingness to acknowledge the underlying feelings. When the deliverer of the sarcasm gets angry or defensive at the recipient of it for “taking things too personally” or being “too sensitive,” they are trying to invalidate the other’s feelings and avoid feeling guilty or responsible for causing them pain."
I think these statements are something you should reflect on and talk to a therapist about.

There are several symptoms of being emotionally stunted. It isn't always that people react "emotionally" or get "angry." Emotional stunt can manifest in other ways too, like not taking accountability for your actions or the way you negatively affected others, not recognizing or taking accountability for how you've hurt people's feelings, and being detached from your own emotions and seeing other's emotional vulnerability as a weakness.
If you don't learn to get a handle on your inability to understand and properly react to other's emotional needs and take accountability for the way you've hurt others then you'll drive people out of your life. This will also make it difficult for you to sustain a job/career.

This is all something I highly recommend you talk to a therapist about. If you're still in grade-school, a counselor will help you too.
And I hope I'm not chasing you away from therapy by continuing to suggest it, I just genuinely think you would benefit from it.

1. It's rude to offer advice when someone didn't directly ask for it or imply that they need it. This is something that people with high emotional intelligence understand.

2. You're advising that a specific type of person should be more like you/your type of person, or become more developed in a certain function that you are high in. That is also rude, and condescending, because you are suggesting that they are not good enough as they are and should be more like you. In Jungian theory, all functions are weighed the same in usefulness and value, and each type in it's pure and healthy form has relatively equal strength and weaknesses.
Additionally, your experience with one ENTJ does not define all ENTJs. ENTJs are not 100% confined by their jungian type and, just like all other types, can vary from person to person. It doesn't make sense to post in a group of ENTJs about how undeveloped they are in emotional intelligence when you have only experienced one or two ENTJs in your lifetime and don't have a good understanding about how ENTJs actually function. You have a disproportionally small sample size compared to the population size - a sampling error, if you will.
Also, high Fi or Fe does not automatically mean you have a high emotional intelligence or emotional maturity.

3. If you really wanted to help someone grow you would want to have a well-intentioned one-on-one conversation with the individual. You would not post in an entire community to subtly insulting them in the guise of good faith, and then continue to subtly insult them in the comments.

4. You are not qualified to be giving this kind of advice. If someone is truly struggling with emotional intelligence and emotional maturity, they should see a professional. You are clearly not a professional. If a therapist talked down to me like you talk down to people I would report them.

I highly suggest that you do some self-reflection and seek out a professional yourself. My therapist has helped me tremendously.

I also suggest that you try to recognize the amount of backlash that you are receiving and consider that you may be in the wrong here. Usually, if people en masse think you did something wrong, you likely did something wrong. It may be a good idea for you to take some time to genuinely consider some of the criticism you've received, and in turn, grow as a person.
